title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: The Plumbing of 3X Leverage: Creation Units, Swap Supply Chains, and Fee Waterfalls

epigraph.quote: In leveraged ETFs, liquidity is manufactured on the primary market and leased on the secondary market.
epigraph.author: ETF Capital Markets Handbook

web_blocks.html: KORU's distribution model and supply chain operate through the two-tier ETF ecosystem [1][2]. It requires no physical warehouses or enterprise sales forces [1]. On the primary market, Authorized Participants (APs) create and redeem shares directly with the Direxion Shares ETF Trust [1]. These institutional market makers transact in large Creation Unit blocks using cash or in-kind baskets of EWY [1]. In FY2025, in-kind redemptions generated $17,807,686 in realized gains for the fund [1]. Under IRC Section 852(b)(6), these in-kind transfers are generally non-taxable at the fund level [1]. This institutional mechanism shields remaining shareholders from capital gains distributions on the physical EWY sleeve [1]. Meanwhile, the secondary market handles public trading on NYSE Arca [6]. There, average daily volume reached 32.57 million shares across an AUM base of $985.42 million [6].

KORU's upstream supply chain centers on the over-the-counter total return swap market [1]. The fund holds a 50.9% physical EWY sleeve [1]. Therefore, it requires ~249% synthetic leverage to achieve its 300% daily exposure target [1]. To source this exposure, Rafferty Asset Management partners with four Tier-1 prime-broker counterparties [1]. These institutions are Bank of America Merrill Lynch (SOFR + 60 bps), Barclays (SOFR + 70 bps), J.P. Morgan (SOFR + 70 bps), and Citibank N.A. (SOFR + 85 bps) [1]. Multi-dealer diversification prevents single-counterparty credit bottlenecks if one bank restricts balance-sheet capacity during market turmoil [1]. Even so, this synthetic architecture carries an ongoing funding spread [1][2]. Financing costs on the swap book sit roughly 60 to 85 basis points above SOFR [1]. That financing cost embeds directly into daily swap resets, beyond the headline 0.95% operating expense cap [1][2].

web_blocks.title: The Hidden Unit Cost: Prospectus AFFE vs. Audited Total Expense Ratio
paragraphs: Investors often underestimate KORU's fee drag by reviewing only Rafferty's 0.95% Operating Expense Limitation Agreement [2]. In practice, KORU bears three distinct layers of explicit cost [1][2]. First, capped fund operating expenses equal 0.95% [1][2]. This figure includes a 0.75% advisory fee, a 0.05% management service fee, and fund administration [1]. Second, Acquired Fund Fees and Expenses (AFFE) from holding EWY raise the prospectus net expense ratio to 1.32% [2][6]. Third, audited broker interest expense pushed KORU's FY2025 total net expense ratio to 1.68% of average net assets [1]. On top of these explicit costs, OTC swap contracts embed an implicit spread of SOFR plus 60 to 85 basis points [1].

web_blocks.html: From a sponsor perspective, KORU provides a high-margin, scalable fee business for Rafferty Asset Management [1]. Under Note 6 of the FY2025 Form N-CSR, the advisory fee is 0.75% of average daily net assets up to $1.5 billion [1]. It steps down to 0.70% between $1.5B and $2.0B, and 0.55% above $3.0B [1]. The fund also pays a 0.05% management services fee [1]. When average net assets hovered near ~$20M–$26M in FY2022–FY2023, fixed listing and audit costs exceeded the 0.95% expense cap [1]. Those overages required small adviser reimbursements [1]. As net assets expanded to $240.60M in FY2025 and $985.42M in 2026, fixed costs shrank as a percentage of assets [1][6]. Consequently, the adviser recouped $35,356 of previously waived fees [1]. At ~$985M in AUM, KORU generates approximately $7.4M–$7.9M in annualized management fees with minimal incremental overhead [1][6].

Daily rebalancing creates an invisible transaction-friction and roll-cost layer for fund holders [2][5]. Whenever KORU gains 6% during a strong Seoul trading session, its leverage ratio drops below 300% [2][5]. Portfolio managers must buy additional EWY swap notional into the 4:00 PM ET close to restore 3x exposure [1][2]. Conversely, when KORU drops 6%, managers must sell swap notional into market weakness [2][5]. Prime brokers absorb most routine execution within agreed SOFR plus 60 to 85 basis point spreads [1]. However, extreme single-day index moves force dealers to widen hedging spreads [1][5]. This dynamic subtly compounds the total cost of holding KORU through volatile macro environments [1][5].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand how KORU actually works as a business—both for the sponsor that runs it and for the trader who rents it—you have to look at two different sets of unit economics side by side. On one side is Rafferty Asset Management, which collects a clean, asset-based toll. On the other side is the fund itself, which has to pay Wall Street swap dealers for leverage while earning yield on its cash collateral.

Start with the distribution and supply chain. KORU does not have a salesforce knocking on doors in Seoul or New York. Its primary-market distribution runs through Authorized Participants—institutional market makers who create and redeem large blocks of KORU shares whenever secondary-market demand on NYSE Arca pushes the trading price away from intraday net asset value. In FY2025, those in-kind redemptions generated $17.81 million in realized gains inside the fund, a structural tax shield that kept KORU from having to pass big capital-gains distributions to shareholders on its physical EWY sleeve. Meanwhile, secondary-market liquidity has become formidable: on an asset base that reached $985.42 million, KORU trades an average of 32.57 million shares a day.

Now follow the cash waterfall inside the fund itself using the audited FY2025 Statement of Operations. In fiscal year 2025, KORU collected $3.81 million in cash investment income—$1.59 million from EWY dividends and $2.22 million from Treasury and government money market interest. Against that $3.81 million, the fund paid $0.78 million in direct broker interest expense (roughly 20.5% of investment income), $0.81 million in investment advisory fees to Rafferty at the 0.75% statutory rate, and $0.22 million in net licensing, management service, and administrative costs. That left $2.00 million—or $52.60 out of every $100 of cash income—as net investment income.

That positive $2.00 million net investment income number might fool a casual reader into thinking KORU pays for itself. It does not, for two reasons you must keep front and center. First, as short-term U.S. interest rates fluctuate, the 4% money market yield that subsidized FY2025 expenses can shrink—look back to FY2021, when near-zero T-bill yields left KORU with negative net investment income of -$2.70 per share. Second, the explicit 1.68% audited net expense ratio (or 1.32% prospectus ratio including Acquired Fund Fees and Expenses from EWY) does not capture the implicit financing spread baked into the daily swap resets—SOFR plus 60 to 85 basis points across Bank of America, Citibank, Barclays, and J.P. Morgan—nor does it capture the quadratic volatility drag of daily rebalancing.

Think as well about the operational leverage on the other side of the table—for Rafferty Asset Management. When KORU's net assets languished at $20.09 million in FY2022 and $26.05 million in FY2023, fixed annual overhead like exchange listing fees ($10,087 in FY2025), MSCI licensing fees ($72,621), and audit fees ate into the 0.95% expense cap, forcing Rafferty to reimburse the fund. By FY2025, with net assets at $240.60 million, those same fixed costs became a rounding error—and by late 2026, at $985.42 million in AUM, Rafferty's 0.75% advisory fee plus 0.05% management service fee generates nearly $8 million a year in high-margin revenue.

Finally, remember what happens at 3:55 PM Eastern Time every single day. Because KORU must reset to exactly 300% exposure, every up-day forces the fund to buy more swap notional into the close, and every down-day forces it to sell swap notional into the close. That daily 'buy high, sell low' mechanical flow is the hidden supply-chain friction of all leveraged ETFs: it guarantees 3x exposure for tomorrow morning's open, but it turns every choppy week into a slow leak of capital.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The unit economics of KORU reveal a classic asymmetry between sponsor and holder. For Rafferty Asset Management, scaling KORU from $20 million in FY2022 to $240.6 million in FY2025 and nearly $1 billion in 2026 turns an 80-basis-point fee stream into a high-margin annuity. For the fund holder, every 1% of explicit fee plus swap spread is compounded against daily path variance—meaning the true cost of ownership is low over a three-day swing and punishing over a choppy three-year hold.

section_takeaway: KORU's FY2025 audited cash waterfall shows $3.81M in dividend/collateral income covering $1.80M in net expenses ($2.00M NII), but true holder cost combines a 1.32%–1.68% explicit expense drag with SOFR+60–85 bps swap spreads and daily volatility decay [1][2].
